a dynamically defined capability for a fresh, non-reserved, non-colliding namespace is admitted exactly as a statically declared one would be
acceptance[2]: a dynamic package cannot provide a service in the reserved dsh.* namespace
acceptance[2]: a dynamic package cannot listen on an event in the reserved dsh.* namespace
acceptance[2]: a dynamic package cannot register a tool name a statically loaded plugin already owns
acceptance[2]: two dynamic packages carry distinct plugin identities, so one cannot claim the other's tool

entries.note: acceptance[2]: '动态 Cordis 定义同样受规则约束.' Covered across tools, services and events for the dynamic origin, through the real runner's guard facade rather than a hand-built context. The distinct-identities case is load-bearing rather than incidental: registrations previously resolved to Fiber.name -- the name the model wrote in its own source -- which is forgeable, and under a Loader every dynamic half hangs beneath one shared cordis-dynamic group entry, collapsing every dynamic package into a single owner and making dynamic-vs-dynamic collision undetectable. KNOWN RESIDUAL, recorded rather than covered: static-origin service and event registration remains ungated, since ctx.provide and ctx.on live in vendor/cordis behind the unlanded Fiber fix. must[0] is enforced as Tool across all origins, Service/Event for the dynamic origin only. This clause's coverage is therefore complete for dynamic definitions, which is what it names, and the static residual belongs to whoever lands that fix.

coveredBy.title: lists a non-terminal Run reconstructed from the durable store by a fresh service
lists every non-terminal Run, not just the most recently written one
omits a Run that reached a terminal state before the restart from the non-terminal listing
resumes a non-terminal Run reconstructed after a restart
lists the Run a previous boot left behind as non-terminal, so a restart can resume it
a store document naming a Run state outside the closed set is refused, never restored and offered for resumption
CHARACTERIZATION: a corrupt store document is refused loudly, never read as an empty registry

entries.note: acceptance[0]: '进程重启后可列出所有非终态 Run 并恢复.' The Provider stage proves the happy path with a restart modelled as a fresh store AND a fresh service over the same path, sharing nothing but the file, so an in-memory double cannot pass. The Usage case proves it on a real harness boot. The Fault stage adds what a clean restart cannot: a DAMAGED store must not satisfy this clause by restoring a Run in a state outside must[0]'s closed set and offering it for resumption -- listNonTerminalRuns treats any non-terminal state as resumable and resumeRun re-stamps ownerId, MASKING a foreign owner, so nothing downstream would have caught it. The characterization case pins that a corrupt document is refused loudly rather than read as an empty registry, which would satisfy 'listed every non-terminal Run' vacuously by listing none.

coveredBy.title: accepted -> waiting is rejected
succeeded -> running is rejected
cancelled -> cancelled is rejected
rejects an illegal transition through the service, naming the exact rejected pair
writes nothing for a rejected transition: the restored Run keeps its state and its unextended event log
two concurrent transitions out of one state never both succeed, and the durable log records exactly the accepted one

entries.note: acceptance[1]: '非法状态转换被拒绝.' The Contract stage settles it exhaustively -- a 10x10 sweep over every ordered state pair, derived from the real LEGAL_RUN_TRANSITIONS table, so every legal edge has a passing case and every illegal pair a rejected one; three representatives are cited here rather than all 100. The Provider stage proves the rejection survives the durable boundary and, critically, that a refused transition WRITES NOTHING. The Fault case closes the gap none of those reach: two CONCURRENT transitions out of one state. Before the fix both were accepted -- one to planning and one to cancelled -- and the append-only log ended holding only the second, so an accepted transition vanished and the service admitted two mutually exclusive exits from one state. A per-state-pair table cannot express that; only concurrency can.

coveredBy.title: the same Session id seeds two independently created Runs
attachSessionToRun appends an additional Session/Agent, so one Run spans multiple Sessions
associates one Session with multiple Runs across a restart
spans one Run across multiple Sessions durably: an attached Session survives a restart
opens an independent Run per agent session, so one Session never joins another Session's Run

entries.note: acceptance[2]: '一个 Session 可关联多个 Run,一个 Run 可跨多个 Session/Agent.' Both directions of the many-to-many relation are covered, and both are proven to survive a restart rather than only holding in memory -- which matters because the clause is about durable association, not a transient one. The Usage case adds the negative half the positive cases cannot establish: a real boot opens an INDEPENDENT Run per agent session, so the relation is genuinely many-to-many rather than one Run silently collecting every session.

coveredBy.title: must[1]: an untrusted workspace permits only safe reads and denies every project plugin/hook/MCP-server/executable-skill/home-profile-patch-override load
gate: an untrusted workspace denies project instructions, so opening a clone never reads the repository's own AGENTS.md

a trusted-read workspace (never upgraded to trusted-execute) still denies every project-level executable load kind, so opening the clone alone can never reach a subprocess/network/credential-read path
offers the model neither the clone's executable skills nor its instructions while the workspace is untrusted
offers no skill from a cloned repository while the workspace is untrusted, and still offers the host-owned skill

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'cloning a repository carrying malicious configuration and opening it produces no subprocess, no network access, and no credential read.' Evidenced by denial at the load decision rather than by observing the absence of a syscall: a freshly opened clone binds at untrusted (P-stage), and untrusted denies every project-level executable load kind -- plugins, hooks, MCP servers, executable skills, and home/profile patch overrides -- which are the only paths by which opening a workspace could reach a subprocess, the network, or a credential. The C-stage case names that closure explicitly for trusted-read, the state one step above untrusted, so the guarantee is not an artefact of the lowest state alone. The two U-stage cases prove the denial at the model-visible surface: the clone's skills and instructions are absent from what the model is offered. NEGATIVE-SPACE CONTROL: the U-stage pair is load-bearing only because its positive twin ('offers the model both the clone's executable skills and its instructions once that same clone is granted trusted-execute', cited under acceptance[2]) proves the fixture can offer them at all, so the absence measures a trust decision rather than an empty fixture.

coveredBy.title: directory replaced: the same canonical path reporting a different device/inode demotes an existing trusted-execute record to untrusted
symlink retargeted: a different canonical path demotes an existing trusted-execute record to untrusted even when device/inode happen to match
directory moved: a different canonical path with the same device/inode still demotes an existing trusted-execute record to untrusted
drops trust when the workspace directory is replaced in place under the same canonical path
drops trust when the symlink the workspace was opened through is retargeted to another directory
does not carry trust to the new canonical path of a moved directory that kept its inode
drops a granted workspace to untrusted once the directory at that path is replaced, and does not re-grant it from configuration
drops a granted workspace to untrusted once the symlink it was opened through is retargeted to another directory
CHARACTERIZATION: drops trust when the device id changes while the canonical path and inode do not

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'trust is not inherited automatically after the directory is replaced, the symlink is retargeted, or the directory is moved.' All three named mutations are covered at three independent layers: the C-stage reconciliation decision, the P-stage provider observing a real filesystem, and the U-stage resolution that a Consumer sees. The three are not redundant -- each mutation defeats a different subset of the identity tuple (canonical path, device, inode, creation time), and the case titles state which, so a reconciliation that checked only one component would still fail at least one of them. The U-stage replacement case additionally asserts the workspace is NOT re-granted from configuration, closing the path where trust returns through a config read rather than through inheritance. POSITIVE CONTROL: 'an unchanged identity (same canonical path, device, and inode) preserves the current trust state and grantor' (C) and 'keeps host-granted trust across a re-observation of an unchanged directory' (P) prove reconciliation is not simply dropping trust unconditionally -- without them, a reconcile that always returned untrusted would satisfy every case above.

coveredBy.title: downgrading from trusted-execute to trusted-read revokes exactly the five project-level executable kinds and keeps project instructions, which trusted-read still injects
downgrading from trusted-read to untrusted revokes exactly project-instructions, the one kind trusted-read granted that untrusted does not
offers the model both the clone's executable skills and its instructions once that same clone is granted trusted-execute
must[2]: downgradeTrust refuses a raising target, so acceptance[2] entry point can never grant trusted-execute with no host principal and no audit record
must[2]: downgradeTrust refuses a raising target even when the presented record still carries a grantor from an earlier grant
CHARACTERIZATION: downgrading a workspace that never granted anything revokes nothing and invents no grantor

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'downgrading trust immediately revokes project capabilities.' The two C-stage cases assert EXACT revocation sets at both downgrade steps, not merely that something was revoked: trusted-execute to trusted-read revokes the five executable kinds and keeps project instructions, and trusted-read to untrusted revokes exactly project-instructions. An over-broad implementation that revoked everything on any downgrade would fail both. The F-stage pair closes the direction of this same entry point -- BEFORE that stage, downgradeTrust accepted a RAISING target, so acceptance[2]'s own entry point could mint a trusted-execute record with no host principal and no audit, bypassing must[2]; the second case proves the refusal holds even when the presented record carries a grantor from an earlier legitimate grant. The characterization case fixes the no-op boundary so a downgrade of a never-granted workspace cannot fabricate a grantor. POSITIVE CONTROL: the U-stage case proves the capabilities being revoked are genuinely offered at trusted-execute, so revocation is measured against a real grant.

coveredBy.title: walking every page via nextCursor from an absent cursor to exhaustion returns every session exactly once, for page size 5000
walking every page via nextCursor from an absent cursor to exhaustion returns every session exactly once, for page size 1
paginates correctly when multiple sessions share the exact same createdAt, exercising the id tiebreak rather than relying on createdAt alone to order records
walks every page of a restored listing, visiting each durable record exactly once with no omission or duplication
feeds listSessions, so a tenant-filtered page walk over the real corpus omits and duplicates nothing

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'pagination over a million-session fixture is stable, with no omission or duplication.' Evidenced as the property rather than the fixture size: the C-stage cases walk a generated corpus to exhaustion via nextCursor and assert each session is visited EXACTLY once, across page sizes spanning the extremes (1 and 5000) plus randomized sizes in between, so the invariant is checked at boundary and interior page sizes rather than one convenient value. The same-createdAt case is the one that makes it stable rather than merely correct: without an id tiebreak, records sharing a timestamp can be skipped or repeated across a page boundary, which is exactly the omission/duplication this clause names. P and U carry it through the two layers where a page walk could still break after C proves the algorithm -- a listing restored from the durable store, and one projected from a live corpus.

coveredBy.title: assertNoLegalHold refuses a session under legal hold with LegalHoldBlocksErasureError
assertNoLegalHold refuses a session that is under legal hold AND already soft-deleted, proving disposition never bypasses the hold check
a session with no legal hold is admitted: assertNoLegalHold's proof authorizes a real hardErase call all the way through
persists a legal hold so a fresh service still refuses to hard-erase after a restart
leaves a held record durably intact after a refused erase, rather than partially destroying it

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'a legal hold blocks a hard erase.' The C-stage pair asserts the refusal and closes the bypass route in the same breath -- a held session that is ALSO soft-deleted is still refused, so no disposition value can route around the hold. POSITIVE CONTROL, required because the refusal cases are negative space: 'a session with no legal hold is admitted' proves the guard is a decision rather than a function that denies everything; without it, an assertNoLegalHold that always threw would satisfy both refusals. The P-stage pair adds what C cannot show: the hold survives a restart (a hold that lived only in memory would refuse nothing after a crash), and a refused erase leaves the record DURABLY INTACT rather than partially destroyed -- refusing after destroying half the dependents would satisfy a naive 'was it refused' assertion.

coveredBy.title: HARD_ERASE_POLICY destroys all four target kinds completely, matching acceptance[2]

an authorized hardErase (no legal hold) reaches all four dependent-store kinds, in order, with the full real target shape per kind -- not just kind order -- matching must[2]'s standalone propagateDeletion(HARD_ERASE_POLICY) rigor
SOFT_DELETE_POLICY only hides the query index, leaving attachments/memory/artifacts untouched
propagates an authorized erase to all four dependent stores and removes the record durably
does not resurrect an erased record for a fresh service over the same path

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'an authorized erase propagates completely.' Completeness is asserted as all four dependent-store kinds reached with the full target shape per kind, not merely as call order -- a propagation that visited the right stores with wrong targets would pass an order-only assertion. CONTRAST CONTROL: SOFT_DELETE_POLICY touching ONLY the query index is what makes 'complete' meaningful; a propagation that always destroyed everything would satisfy the hard-erase cases while being catastrophically wrong, and this pair is what separates the two policies. The P-stage cases add durability: propagation reaches the real stores, and the erased record does not come back for a fresh service over the same path -- a propagation that removed rows without committing would look complete in-process.

coveredBy.title: a corruption partway through the log recovers only the valid prefix before it, plus evidence -- never a line after it, even one that is individually well-formed
a corruption at the very first line leaves no recoverable prefix at all, returning evidence with no events
a fully valid log with no corruption reads back completely, with no partial-recovery evidence
enforcement: recovery stops at the first unreadable row and never resumes past it, even when later rows parse
enforcement: the evidence names the exact row and reason, not a summary
control: a log whose every row parses recovers fully, so the truncation cases below measure a decision

entries.note: acceptance[3]: 'a corrupted-log read returns the minimal recoverable range and evidence.' Both halves are asserted separately. MINIMALITY: recovery stops at the first unreadable row and never resumes past it even when later rows are individually well-formed -- a reader that skipped the bad row and continued would produce a LONGER range that is not the minimal recoverable one, and would silently mix records whose interpretation the corruption may have invalidated. The first-row case pins the boundary where 'minimal' means nothing at all, which must not report as an empty success. EVIDENCE: the exact row number and parse reason, not a summary. POSITIVE CONTROL: a fully valid log reads back complete with NO partial-recovery evidence, so the truncation cases measure a decision rather than a reader that always truncates. The F stage re-asserts both against the entry point directly, and additionally records two defects it does not repair.

coveredBy.title: finds a two-package cycle
finds a four-package cycle and reports the shortest cycle when a shorter one also exists
accepts a cycle covered by a declared exemption and still rejects an undeclared one
excludes devDependencies from the production graph acceptance[0] scopes
reports zero violations and no unexempted cycle in the production package graph
calibration: the same entry point reports a violation when one exists, so zero distinguishes this repository from a broken check

entries.note: acceptance[0]: 'the production package graph has no unexempted cycle.' The detection cases prove the search finds cycles at two sizes and honours the exemption store in both directions (an exempted cycle accepted, an undeclared one still rejected), and the devDependencies case fixes the graph's scope -- 'production' excludes dev edges, so a checker including them would report cycles this clause does not name. The real-repository case is the clause's actual assertion. CALIBRATION, which is what makes that zero mean anything: the F-stage case runs the SAME entry point against a fixture root and requires a real violation, so 'zero violations here' is distinguishable from 'this function never reports violations'. An always-zero verdict and a working verdict produce identical reports without it.

coveredBy.title: rejects a kernel dependency on a surfaces-apps package and on a providers package
permits a kernel package importing only Context, and rejects one importing Service
rejects a forbidden Cordis binding imported type-only, since rule 4 grants the kernel no type-only escape
resolves the real trust-kernel Cordis edge as permitted under rule 4 and its dsh-invariants edge as allowlisted
enforcement: a kernel upward edge is a violation even when it is the narrow event-type kind
control: the same narrow event-type edge from a non-kernel layer IS allowed, proving the case above measures the kernel rule

entries.note: acceptance[1]: 'any kernel dependency on Cordis, UI, or a concrete model provider fails.' Covered as the kernel having NO escape hatch, which is the only way the clause is stronger than an ordinary upward-edge rule. Three routes are closed independently: an ordinary upward edge to surfaces-apps and to providers; a Cordis binding beyond the single permitted Context; and the same forbidden binding imported type-only, since a type-only import is the obvious way to argue an edge is harmless. The F stage closes the fourth: must[1]'s narrow event-type allowance, which is a real exception everywhere else, does not apply to the kernel. POSITIVE CONTROL: the identical event-type edge from a non-kernel layer IS allowed, so the kernel case measures the kernel rule rather than a suite that rejects event-type edges generally -- and 'permits a kernel importing only Context' proves the Cordis rule is a binding-level decision, not a blanket ban that would make the permitted mechanism unusable.

coveredBy.title: finds a four-package cycle and reports the shortest cycle when a shorter one also exists
calibration: the real scan reaches real input — hundreds of packages, thousands of edges
completes within the 10-second production-scale budget on a dense, many-overlapping-cycle graph (acceptance[2])
finds the real shortest cycle even when a longer, disjoint cycle is encountered first in construction order

entries.note: acceptance[2]: 'the check completes within 10 seconds and reports the shortest cycle path.' Two independent requirements. SHORTEST: asserted where a shorter cycle also exists, so returning any cycle is insufficient -- a search reporting the first cycle found would pass a single-cycle fixture and fail this one. WITHIN 10s: the C-stage case times a 300-package scan against the budget. CALIBRATION of that timing claim: the F-stage case asserts the real scan reaches real input (>200 packages, >1000 edges, zero unclassified), because a scan that completes quickly by examining nothing satisfies a timing assertion perfectly. The budget only means something once the work it bounds is shown to have happened.
